### Mean-zero noise model {#sec-noise-model}

Measurement noise is almost always modeled as a random variable
$\noise$ with **mean zero** and variance $\varpar$.

Mean zero is a parametrization choice, not a substantive assumption.
In $Y = f(x) + \noise$, moving a constant from $\noise$ into $f(x)$
changes the split but not the distribution of $Y$,
so the data identify only the sum $f(x) + \E{\noise}$, the mean of $Y$ at $x$.
Requiring $\E{\noise} = 0$ picks the one split in which $f(x)$ is that mean.
It costs nothing provided the model for $f$ can absorb a constant,
as any model with an intercept can.
It restricts the model only when $f$ cannot absorb one,
as in a regression through the origin.

That choice buys one identity, used repeatedly across statistical modeling
and machine learning.
